title: Urine, Blood, and Swab Specimens

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the concepts and purposes of urine, blood, and swab specimen collection, including clean-catch, timed, and sterile techniques.
- Select the appropriate containers, additives, transport media, and labeling for different specimen types and tests.
- Apply standard precautions and bloodborne pathogen infection-prevention practices, including PPE, hand hygiene, sharps safety, and spill cleanup.
- Support collection through preparation, patient instructions, documentation, and verification, escalating to licensed staff whenever a task exceeds the assistant's training or authorization.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the assistant as a lab helper who sets out the cups and labels and follows the teacher's exact steps, but the teacher decides what to test and reads the answer key.

### Question 2

Before collecting anything, the assistant checks two things about the person — like their full name and birthday — so the sample is never mixed up with someone else's.

### Question 3

Washing hands or using hand gel before and after touching samples is like washing your hands before and after handling food — it keeps germs from spreading.

### Question 4

The assistant treats every blood sample like it might have germs, because you can't tell just by looking at someone whether they are carrying something.

### Question 5

The assistant writes the person's name and info on the cup right away, before walking away, so it can't get mixed up with anyone else's cup.

### Question 6

The urine goes into a clean cup that won't leak and has a tight lid, with the person's name written on it.

### Question 7

For a clean-catch sample, the person cleans the area and starts peeing, then catches the middle part in the cup so skin germs don't get in.

### Question 8

The assistant puts on gloves any time they might touch blood or body fluids, just like wearing an apron when handling something messy.

### Question 9

After using a needle, the assistant drops it straight into a special hard box for sharp things, without putting the cap back on.

### Question 10

Sharp things go in a special hard, leak-proof box that says it is for sharp, germy items.

### Question 11

If things might splash, the assistant wears a face shield and apron on top of gloves, like a painter covering up before spraying paint.

### Question 12

The biohazard picture is a warning sign that says 'careful, this might have germs' — treat it like a 'wet paint' sign.

### Question 13

The sample cup goes inside a second sealed bag, like putting a drink in a spill-proof pouch so it can't leak in your bag.

### Question 14

The tube has a mark, and it must be filled to that mark so the right amount of blood mixes with the special powder inside — like following a recipe's exact amounts.

### Question 15

The assistant gently tips the tube over and back a few times, like gently stirring, instead of shaking it hard like a soda bottle.

### Question 16

The swab is put in a little gel or liquid 'lunchbox' that keeps the tiny germs alive on the way to the lab.

### Question 17

The name label goes on the cup itself, not the lid, because lids can come off and get swapped like pen caps.

### Question 18

The assistant double-checks that the name on the cup matches the name on the paper order, like matching a name tag to a permission slip.

### Question 19

The first pee of the morning has been sitting in the bladder all night, so it is stronger, which makes some tests easier to read.

### Question 20

The assistant writes down what was collected and when, right away, like writing the time and date on a homework assignment.

### Question 21

When the assistant is not sure what to do, they ask the teacher (the clinician or supervisor) instead of guessing.

### Question 22

After taking off gloves, the assistant washes or sanitizes their hands, because germs can sneak onto hands even under gloves.

### Question 23

After using the collection area, the assistant wipes it down with cleaning spray, like wiping a table after eating.

### Question 24

If a needle pokes them, the assistant washes the spot right away and tells the person in charge immediately, like telling a teacher about a cut.

### Question 25

A random sample is just 'pee in this cup whenever you need to,' while a timed sample is 'collect at this exact time.'

### Question 26

The tubes are filled in a special order so the powder in one tube doesn't sneak into the next tube and mess up its test.

### Question 27

The powder in some tubes works like the 'anti-freeze' of blood — it keeps the blood from turning solid (clotting) so the test can use it liquid.

### Question 28

If blood is left to turn into jelly (clot), the watery part on top is serum; if a powder keeps it liquid, the watery part is plasma — plasma still has the 'clotting' ingredients, serum used them up.

### Question 29

The purple-top tube has a powder that stops blood from clumping, which is what the 'count the blood cells' test needs.

### Question 30

The person wipes clean, starts peeing, and catches only the middle squirt in the cup, being careful not to touch the inside.

### Question 31

The patient should be careful not to touch the inside of the cup and to catch the middle part, like catching rain in a clean cup without touching the inside.

### Question 32

To collect for a whole day, the patient first empties the bladder and throws that away, then saves every single drop for the next full day and night.

### Question 33

The big collection jug stays cool in the fridge, like keeping leftovers cold so they don't go bad.

### Question 34

The swab should touch the back of the throat near the tonsils, not the tongue or teeth, so it only picks up the germs we are looking for.

### Question 35

The swab stays in its wrapper until the very moment it touches the wound, then goes straight into its little tube, like keeping a clean toothbrush wrapped until you use it.

### Question 36

Because swabbing the nose can make someone sneeze, the assistant wears gloves and a face shield, like wearing goggles when something might spray.

### Question 37

If a patient starts to faint, the assistant tells the clinician right away and helps keep the person from falling, like catching a friend who goes dizzy.

### Question 38

If a bruise appears after a blood draw, the assistant tells the clinician, like pointing out a new mark to the teacher instead of hiding it.

### Question 39

Keeping the tight band on too long is like pinching a hose — the blood backs up and gets too thick in one spot, which changes the numbers.

### Question 40

The germ-growing bottles are filled first and very carefully, so no stray germs from skin or other tubes get in and confuse the test.

### Question 41

Blood cells are like tiny water balloons; shaking the tube too hard pops them, which ruins the sample.

### Question 42

Some samples are like milk — they spoil if left out — so they are kept cold on the way to the lab.

### Question 43

Some samples are like photographs — light ruins them — so they get wrapped in a dark cover like a blanket.

### Question 44

Fresh urine should be warm like the body; checking the temperature is a way to make sure the sample really just came from the person.

### Question 45

If the urine can't go to the lab right away, the assistant keeps it cold, like putting leftovers in the fridge instead of leaving them out.

### Question 46

If a sample spills, the assistant puts on gloves and cleans it up with the right cleaner, like cleaning up a mess in the kitchen with gloves and spray.

### Question 47

The assistant uses a broom and dustpan or tongs to pick up broken glass, never their hands, and then cleans the floor.

### Question 48

The sharp-box gets swapped for a new one when it is about three-quarters full, before anything can poke out.

### Question 49

The assistant wears gloves and carefully pours the pee into the labeled cup, like pouring juice without dripping, then cleans up.

### Question 50

Getting urine from a catheter is done super-cleanly to keep germs out, and the assistant helps the clinician instead of doing it alone.

### Question 51

For a baby, a sticky collection bag is placed over the diaper area to catch the pee, kind of like a special sticker-pouch.

### Question 52

For a fasting sugar test, the patient doesn't eat anything (except water) for several hours before the blood draw, like not snacking before a weigh-in.

### Question 53

This test is done exactly two hours after the person finishes eating, like setting a timer after lunch.

### Question 54

If the tube isn't filled to the line, there is too much powder for the small amount of blood, like using a whole packet of drink mix in a tiny cup of water.

### Question 55

The label has the person's full name and birthday, plus the date, time, and who collected it — like a name tag with all the important details.

### Question 56

If the name on the cup doesn't match the name on the order form, the assistant stops and asks the person in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 57

If a sample leaks in the bag, the assistant cleans it up safely with gloves and tells the supervisor, like reporting a spill in the lunchroom.

### Question 58

If the tube isn't mixed right away, the blood can turn into jelly (clot), and then the test can't use it.

### Question 59

If the blood went in the wrong tube, the assistant tells the clinician so a new sample can be taken correctly, instead of trying to fix it by hand.

### Question 60

If the sample looks ruined (jelly-like or too little), the assistant tells the clinician so a new one can be taken, instead of sending a bad sample.

### Question 61

The swab stays in its little gel tube so the germs don't dry out and die before the lab can look at them.

### Question 62

The urine for a germ test goes in the fridge if it can't reach the lab right away, so the germs don't grow extra while waiting.

### Question 63

If a patient can't pee when needed, the assistant tells the clinician and helps as directed, like asking the teacher for help.

### Question 64

The assistant makes sure the cap is screwed on tight, like making sure a water bottle lid is closed before putting it in a bag.

### Question 65

If the pee looks different from expected, the assistant writes it down and tells the clinician, like pointing out something unusual to the teacher.

### Question 66

When a patient asks what the test results mean, the assistant says 'the doctor will explain that' instead of guessing.

### Question 67

For the germ-growing test, the cup must be extra-clean (sterile), while a regular pee test just needs a clean cup.

### Question 68

The tubes are used in a set order so the powder from one doesn't accidentally travel into the next one and change its test, like not stirring chocolate into the vanilla batter.

### Question 69

To get serum (the watery part after blood jellies), the assistant picks the tube that lets the blood clot, not the one that stops clotting.

### Question 70

If the lab reports a very serious result, the assistant writes it down and tells the clinician right away, like delivering an urgent message to the teacher.

### Question 71

A cup with no name is like a mystery — it must be thrown away and a new one collected, because guessing the name could hurt someone.

### Question 72

If the sample came from the wrong person, the assistant tells the clinician and a new sample is taken from the right person — you never just switch the name tag.

### Question 73

For collecting a whole day's pee, the person gets one big labeled jug, not a tiny cup.

### Question 74

Each test needs the right kind of sample: a sore throat needs a throat swab, a blood test needs blood, and a pee test needs pee.

### Question 75

If the person forgets to save one pee during the day-long collection, the whole thing starts over — like restarting a timed test when you skip a step.

### Question 76

For a baby or child, the assistant gets the right small supplies and helps keep the child calm while the clinician does the procedure.

### Question 77

Some needles have a built-in shield that snaps over the sharp tip, like a cap that covers a marker tip by itself to keep fingers safe.

### Question 78

The exposure control plan is the office's safety rulebook that says how to avoid getting sick from blood and what to do if someone is exposed.

### Question 79

After a poke or splash, the assistant gets a private medical check and any needed tests, following the office's safety rulebook.

### Question 80

Pee left out too long goes bad, like milk left on the counter — it changes and can't be trusted for the test anymore.

### Question 81

A catheter sample is collected with extra-special 'no germs allowed' care because it goes deeper inside, while clean-catch just lowers the germ count.

### Question 82

The assistant wears gloves for a blood draw, and adds a face shield and apron only if things might splash — like adding a raincoat only when it rains.

### Question 83

Chain of custody is like a sign-in sheet that everyone who touches the sample must sign, so we always know who had it and when.

### Question 84

The assistant explains the steps clearly, hands over a labeled container and written directions, and checks that the patient understands, like giving homework instructions twice.

### Question 85

The assistant finishes writing the name on the cup first, then hurries to help with the urgent task — never leaving a cup with no name.
